name: Military Turbofan Engines (Specific Platforms)

header.one_liner: Specific military turbofan engine types powering Indian combat and transport aircraft — the GE F404/F414 family (Tejas), Safran M88 (Rafale), and Rolls-Royce Adour (Jaguar) — each representing a distinct import dependency with different supply-chain risk profiles.
header.maker: GE Aerospace (F404, F414 — US); Safran Aircraft Engines (M88 — France); Rolls-Royce (Adour — UK)

at_a_glance.GE_F404-IN20: Turbofan, ~84 kN dry / ~120 kN with afterburner; powers LCA Tejas Mk-1A; produced by GE Aerospace (Lynn, Massachusetts); India operates ~80+ F404 engines across 83 Tejas Mk-1A order
at_a_glance.GE_F414-INS6: Turbofan, ~98 kN dry / ~144 kN with afterburner; selected for Tejas Mk-2; India signed ToT agreement 2023 for domestic production by HAL; also bid for MRFA competition
at_a_glance.Safran_M88: Turbofan, ~50 kN dry / ~75 kN with afterburner; powers Rafale (IAF 36 aircraft); fitted, operational; France is sole source for spares and overhauls
at_a_glance.Rolls-Royce_Adour: Low-bypass turbofan, ~25 kN dry / ~37 kN with afterburner; powers SEPECAT Jaguar DARIN III (IAF upgraded fleet); increasingly obsolescent with limited spares pipeline
at_a_glance.Key_dependency: F404 (near-term) and F414 (medium-term) are the most critical: they power India's two next-generation fighter programmes (Tejas Mk-1A and Mk-2) with no indigenous alternative
at_a_glance.Operational_domains: Air (all platforms are combat or combat-training aircraft)

what_it_is.prose: While the 'Military Propulsion' dossier covers the broad strategic challenge, this dossier examines the specific engine types powering Indian combat aircraft and their distinct supply-chain risk profiles. The General Electric F404-IN20 turbofan, producing approximately 84 kN dry and 120 kN with afterburner, powers the LCA Tejas Mk-1A — 83 of which have been ordered by the Indian Air Force. India operates over 80 F404 engines, all imported from GE's Lynn, Massachusetts facility. The GE F414-INS6, producing approximately 98 kN dry and 144 kN with afterburner, has been selected for the LCA Tejas Mk-2 and represents a technology transfer pathway: the 2023 India-US agreement provides for HAL to manufacture F414 engines domestically, though the core intellectual property remains with GE. The Safran M88, producing approximately 50 kN dry and 75 kN with afterburner, powers the 36 Indian Air Force Rafale fighters — France is the sole source for engine spares and major overhauls. The Rolls-Royce Adour, a lower-thrust turbofan producing approximately 25 kN dry, powers the upgraded SEPECAT Jaguar DARIN III fleet — an ageing platform with an increasingly obsolescent spares pipeline. Each engine type carries a different supply-chain risk profile: the F404/F414 family (US) is the most consequential given the scale of Tejas production; the M88 (France) is a small fleet but operationally critical for the IAF's most advanced fighter; the Adour (UK) is a diminishing support challenge as the Jaguar fleet winds down.

capability_notes.summary: Four distinct imported engine families power Indian combat aircraft. The GE F404/F414 (US) is the most critical dependency. The Safran M88 (France) is operationally significant for the Rafale fleet. The Rolls-Royce Adour (UK) is a diminishing dependency on the Jaguar.

dimensions.label: Design ownership
dimensions.note: Zero indigenous military turbofan engine design; all four engine types are foreign-designed.

dimensions.label: Production ownership
dimensions.note: HAL has licence-production experience; GE F414 ToT will build domestic production capability, but core IP remains foreign.

dimensions.label: Critical component sovereignty
dimensions.note: Turbine blades, hot-section components, FADEC, and engine core are entirely foreign; no indigenous production.

dimensions.label: Scale / operational reach
dimensions.note: ~200+ imported military engines across four types powering India's entire combat aircraft fleet; the dependency is absolute and operational.

dimensions.label: Export potential
dimensions.note: India re-exports no military turbofan engines; licence terms prohibit re-export.

faq.question: Which specific turbofan engines power Indian combat aircraft?
faq.answer: The LCA Tejas Mk-1A is powered by the General Electric F404-IN20 (US); the Tejas Mk-2 will use the GE F414-INS6 (US, under ToT agreement 2023); the Rafale is powered by the Safran M88-2 (France); and the SEPECAT Jaguar DARIN III uses the Rolls-Royce Adour Mk.821 (UK). All four engine types are fully imported.

faq.question: What is the risk of GE engine supply disruption?
faq.answer: The GE F404 and F414 are produced at GE Aerospace's Lynn, Massachusetts facility. The US-India defence relationship is strong, but any disruption to bilateral relations (e.g. over India's Russia defence ties) could theoretically affect supply. The 2023 F414 ToT agreement provides a degree of supply assurance by establishing domestic production capability, though the timeline for HAL to produce engines independently of GE oversight is uncertain.

faq.question: How long can the Safran M88 fleet be sustained?
faq.answer: The 36 Safran M88-2 engines powering India's Rafale fleet are supported by a France-origin spares and overhaul pipeline. Safran has committed to long-term support, but India has no domestic M88 overhaul capability — all major overhauls must be sent to France. The fleet is small enough that this is manageable, but it represents an ongoing import dependency for as long as the Rafale remains in Indian service.
